query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles, the premelting and melting behavior is governed by kinetically limited atomic mobility due to intrinsic lattice disorder, which produces local compositional fluctuations. These fluctuations create regions with slightly lower bonding strength that initiate local melting (premelting) before the entire particle melts, leading to a broader melting transition than in uniform, single‐component systems.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid-solution nanoparticles of equimolar Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu with a single-phase, disordered FCC structure prepared by, for example, ultrashort-pulse laser ablation of consolidated precursor powders.
generation.intervention: Subject the nanoparticles to a controlled thermal ramp using in situ laser heating (or an equivalent rapid-heating method) while monitoring the structural evolution in real time via techniques such as XRD and XAS.
generation.conditions: Heating from a temperature well below the premelting range up to above the complete melting point (for example, from ~600°C to ~1400°C) at a controlled rate in an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon) to avoid oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Local compositional heterogeneities and restricted atomic diffusion within the high-entropy matrix.
generation.mechanism: The high degree of chemical complexity and lattice distortion in HEA nanoparticles limits atomic mobility during heating. Consequently, regions with a slightly lower local melting point (due to stochastic variations in element distribution) begin to melt first. These liquid regions then serve as nucleation sites that gradually coalesce, leading to an overall broadening of the melting transition compared to more homogeneous, single-metal nanoparticles.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline single-metal nanoparticles—which exhibit a sharp, uniform melting transition—the HEA nanoparticles will show an extended premelting regime with the formation of localized liquid domains at temperatures lower than the overall melting point, followed by complete melting at a somewhat higher temperature. This behavior would manifest as a broadened and shifted melting peak in DSC measurements and heterogeneous local structural changes in in situ TEM or XRD studies.
generation.baseline: Single-metal or less chemically complex nanoparticles (e.g., Au, Ag, or Pd nanoparticles) that are known to exhibit uniform and sharper melting transitions.
generation.boundary: This phenomenon is expected to occur in nanoscale high-entropy alloys with a high number of principal elements (five or more) where atomic mobility is kinetically limited. The hypothesis may not apply to bulk HEAs or systems where diffusion is enhanced by other factors (e.g., post-synthesis annealing) that enable more uniform melting behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature onset of localized premelting and the quantitative contribution of each element's local bonding environment remain uncertain and will require detailed spatially resolved characterization to quantify.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct an in situ high-temperature study using TEM combined with XRD and XAS to monitor individual HEA nanoparticles during a controlled heating cycle. Map the local structure and composition spatially to detect the initiation and propagation of liquid domains at the nanoparticle scale.
measurements: Real-time TEM imaging and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) to identify local melting events.
XRD to monitor phase changes and broadening of diffraction peaks.
XAS to probe changes in the local bonding environment of constituent elements.
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to record the broadness and onset temperatures of melting peaks.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA nanoparticles melt uniformly with a single, sharp transition (similar to that observed in single-metal nanoparticles) and no evidence of localized premelting or heterogeneous melting domains is observed, then the hypothesis that limited atomic mobility and local compositional fluctuations govern the premelting process would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractInvestigation into non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys has grown in recent years due to questions about the role of entropy stabilization in forming single-phase solid solutions. Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Here, we are motivated by the natural phenomena of crystal growth and equilibrium conditions to introduce a method of HEA development where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated by cooling an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu alloy from the melt steadily over 3 days (cooling rate ~4 °C/h). The result is an alloy containing large Cr-rich precipitates and an almost Cr-free matrix exhibiting compositions within the MnFeCoNiCu system (with trace amounts of Cr). While these studies demonstrate that the relationship between composition and phase stability in HEAs has certainly been considered, expansion beyond the circumstances around the σ-phase has been limited. The further inclusion of processing conditions—the importance of which has been emphasized earlier—to this equation beyond prolonged annealing has not been presented in the literature. Here, we propose a fabrication method applicable to both equiatomic and non-equiatomic HEAs, where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated through a thorough experimental analysis that tests the following hypotheses: For HEAs, an equiatomic composition maximizes configurational entropy, but structure and phase stability are not necessarily optimized. CrMnFeCoNi is not the most stable or preferred alloy composition within the CrMnFeCoNiCu system if the processing conditions (especially a slow cooling rate from the melt) are controlled.

This behavior contrasts with the bimetallic case, suggesting that the rules governing phase formation differ for the systems containing two or five elements: Single-phase alloy formation occurs more readily if more elements are present, as systems that are immiscible on the bimetallic level can be driven to mix by introducing more elements. As the resulting phases of the binary particles cannot readily be explained by their thermodynamic stability, we devised a kinetic model to rationalize the experimental results based on the restrictions imposed by the synthesis. When comparing five-element and two-element mixtures, the concentration of individual atom types is reduced the more elements are present. This will make it increasingly difficult for elements with strong preferences of ordering to form an intermetallic structure or for elements that repulse each other to segregate, simply because they are more dilute. By analyzing the TEM images and EDS elemental mappings (Fig. 1h), all five elements relatively homogeneously are distributed within the CrMnFeCoNi HEA nanoparticles, in which the contents of the Fe, Co and Ni elements are higher than those of the Cr and Mn (Fig. S3), benefiting from their closer reduction potential and fewer valence electrons that form stable compounds while Mn is expected to be partially vaporized during the laser synthesis due to its higher vapor pressure.
